Top 10 stories by votes

  1. Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free

    2372 points · 331 comments · 16 Nov 2026, 20:43 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

The site says self-paced courseware, instant-feedback lessons, badges, and AI tutoring are planned, with several courses scheduled for January 2027.

    Discussion — The project lead described a student-supported effort with human lecture review and invited course requests. Readers welcomed the access but discussed the limits of lecture-only learning, course licensing and attribution, and the role of structured exercises and feedback.

  2. SpaceX catches the Starship to end Flight 15

    Discussion — Commenters focused on the engineering spectacle and on the risks and operational value of catching a large booster at the launch tower. Discussion also covered launch cadence, whether the test objectives justified the approach, and comparisons with other reusable-launch systems.

  4. Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx

    1490 points · 639 comments · 18 Nov 2026, 15:19 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

    Story — Wiz described two HTTP/2-related NGINX vulnerabilities, including an unauthenticated remote-code-execution issue under specific configurations. The report identified affected versions and listed patched NGINX OSS releases, while recommending upgrading or temporarily disabling HTTP/2 during remediation.

    Discussion — Discussion concentrated on exposure and disclosure timing: commenters debated whether public source commits or exploit-branded sites help attackers, and whether disabling HTTP/2 is practical for gRPC and related workloads. Technical replies distinguished the vulnerabilities’ conditions and urged patching.

  7. All AI-generated code should be Open Source

    1285 points · 673 comments · 15 Nov 2026, 14:46 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

    Story — The essay argues that AI-generated code should be open source, citing training on publicly available material and uncertainty around copyrightability of purely AI-generated output. It distinguishes fully automated output from mixed human-and-AI authorship but favors open release for lightly reviewed or prompt-only code.

    Discussion — The dominant response was that public-domain status is not the same as open source: copyright is generally needed to impose open-source license conditions. Commenters also disputed whether AI-assisted code is necessarily uncopyrightable and whether the proposed rule is workable.

  7. Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use

    733 points · 624 comments · 16 Nov 2026, 22:58 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

    Story — The author reverse-engineered Windows 11’s MissionControlAggregator.dll and found telemetry categories for named coding-agent executables, desktop agents, and developer tools. Their testing showed a renamed cmd.exe run as codex.exe set the Codex cohort bit; the article says queued diagnostic data contains categories rather than prompts, source code, or duration-of-use data, and recommends disabling optional diagnostic data to prevent upload.

    Discussion — Commenters debated both the practical case for Linux or reduced reliance on Windows and the significance of the telemetry. Some viewed executable-category logging as unsurprising diagnostics and distinguished local logs from uploaded data; others objected that collection occurs locally before optional upload choices and that categorizing specific AI tools is more intrusive than generic logging.

    709 points · 563 comments · 18 Nov 2026, 00:17 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

Commenters also discussed copyright, citations, paywalls, revenue sharing, Google’s earlier incentives, and whether search should prioritize direct primary sources; the author acknowledged possible commercial-query bias in one dataset.

  10. Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings

    970 points · 556 comments · 16 Nov 2026, 13:39 (Europe/London) · HN discussion

These are the advocacy group’s price-history findings; it calls for recent-low-price disclosure rules for advertised sales.

    Discussion — Commenters described misleading sale pricing as a longstanding retail practice and recommended price-history tools, comparison shopping, wishlists, and direct purchases. They also debated disclosure rules and methodology, noting the promoted-item sample and questions about marketplace versus Amazon pricing, while discussing broader complaints and defenses around Amazon’s search, logistics, returns, and Prime.
